title: Diagnose and Resolve a Stalled Replication Link
summary: Use repadmin to find a stalled inbound replication link and walk the DNS/connectivity/auth decision tree to fix it.
objective: Identify a stalled inbound replication partner and restore replication using the documented, lowest-risk fix for the observed root cause.
prerequisites_detail: Domain Admin rights on a lab domain with at least 2 DCs; RSAT / repadmin available; a lab environment where one DC's network adapter can be safely disabled to simulate the fault.
environment: Two-DC single-domain lab forest (e.g. CONTOSO.LAB), both Windows Server 2022, one designated DC1 (root), one DC2.
topology: DC1 <-> DC2 direct intrasite replication link (default site).
steps: On DC1, run `repadmin /showrepl` and note any partner listed with a non-zero Last Failure Time.
Cross-check with `repadmin /replsummary` for a forest-wide view of largest failure counts.
Check the Directory Service event log on DC1 for Event IDs 1311, 1925, 1988, 2042, 2087, or 2088 around the failure window.
If the failure is a DNS resolution issue (2087/2088), run `nslookup <DC2-GUID>._msdcs.<domain>` from DC1 to confirm the DC locator record resolves.
If the failure is connectivity (1925, RPC port 135 / dynamic range blocked), verify Windows Firewall rules for 'Active Directory Domain Services' are enabled on both DCs.
Once the underlying cause is fixed, force replication with `repadmin /replicate DC1 DC2 <NamingContextDN>` and re-run `repadmin /showrepl` to confirm Last Failure Time resets to 0.
expected_result: repadmin /showrepl on both DCs shows 0 consecutive failures and a recent successful replication timestamp for every partner.
validation: Re-run repadmin /replsummary forest-wide; confirm 0% failure rate; check that a test object created on DC1 is visible on DC2 within one intrasite replication cycle.
rollback: If the applied fix (e.g. a firewall rule change) causes unexpected side effects, revert the specific rule change; this lab makes no destructive changes to AD DS data itself.
cleanup: Remove any test objects created for validation; restore the DC2 network adapter to its normal state if it was used to simulate the fault.

title: View and Gracefully Transfer a FSMO Role
summary: Identify current FSMO role holders and perform a graceful transfer (not a seize) of the RID Master role to another DC.
objective: Correctly identify all five FSMO role holders in a lab forest and transfer the RID Master role to a second DC while the original holder remains online.
prerequisites_detail: Domain Admin (for domain-wide roles) and Enterprise Admin (for forest-wide roles) rights in a 2+ DC lab forest; both DCs online and replicating healthily (verify with OSB-AD-LAB-0001 first).
environment: Two-DC single-domain lab forest, both DCs healthy and replicating.
topology: DC1 (currently holds all five roles, typical for a small lab forest) and DC2 (transfer target).
steps: Run `netdom query fsmo` from any domain-joined machine to list current role holders.

Open PowerShell as Enterprise Admin and run `Get-ADDomain | Select-Object PDCEmulator,RIDMaster,InfrastructureMaster` and `Get-ADForest | Select-Object SchemaMaster,DomainNamingMaster` to confirm via a second method.
Confirm DC1 (current RID Master) and DC2 (target) are both online and show 0 replication failures.
Transfer the RID Master role: `Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole -Identity DC2 -OperationMasterRole RIDMaster`.
Re-run `netdom query fsmo` to confirm DC2 now holds the RID Master role.
expected_result: netdom query fsmo lists DC2 as the RID Master; DC1 no longer holds it.
validation: Create a new test user object on DC1 immediately after transfer to confirm RID pool allocation still functions correctly from the new master.
rollback: Run the same Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole cmdlet targeting DC1 to transfer the role back, since DC1 remains online throughout - this is why transfer (not seize) is the safe path for a planned lab exercise.
cleanup: Delete the test user object created for validation.

title: Forest Recovery Drill: Restore the Forest Root Domain's First DC
summary: A sandbox-only drill: restore one DC in an isolated lab forest's root domain from backup and perform the required authoritative SYSVOL restore.
warning_banner: DESTRUCTIVE / HIGH-BLAST-RADIUS DRILL. Run this ONLY in an isolated lab forest that is never connected to any production network. Never run authoritative SYSVOL restore or forced AD DS restore procedures against a production forest outside a real, declared disaster-recovery event led by your incident process. Ensure the target VM/host is network-isolated (disconnected virtual NIC or an air-gapped host-only network) before starting step 2.
objective: Correctly perform, in isolation, the sequence of a first-DC forest-root recovery: nonauthoritative AD DS restore plus authoritative SYSVOL restore, without connecting the DC to a live network before validation.
prerequisites_detail: A disposable lab forest with at least one full server backup (Windows Server Backup) or system-state backup of the forest root domain's DC; a virtualization host where the target DC's network adapter can be fully disconnected; documented Administrator and DSRM passwords for the lab forest; this lab must never be pointed at a production backup or production DC.
environment: Single isolated lab VM restored from a known-good backup image of a forest-root DC (Windows Server 2022 lab build).
topology: One isolated DC, network-disconnected until validation is complete, no replication partners reachable during the drill.
steps: BACKUP PRECONDITION: confirm a verified, restorable backup of the lab forest-root DC exists and is dated after the last change you want to keep - do not proceed without this.
Disconnect the target VM's virtual network adapter (or otherwise fully isolate it) so it cannot replicate or be reached during recovery.
Boot into Windows Recovery Environment, select System Image Recovery, and restore the full server image per the backup tool's restore wizard.

After the restore completes and the DC restarts (still isolated), perform an authoritative synchronization of the DFSR-replicated SYSVOL using the documented forest-recovery procedure for the first recovered DC in the forest root domain.
Verify AD DS and SYSVOL are internally consistent (dcdiag /v, repadmin /showrepl showing no unexpected partners since it's isolated) before reconnecting to any network.
Only after full verification, reconnect the DC to the isolated lab network segment (still not production) and confirm it advertises itself correctly.
commands: ntdsutil (for authoritative SYSVOL sync per the forest-recovery guide's documented procedure)
expected_result: The restored DC boots cleanly, dcdiag reports no critical errors, and SYSVOL shows itself as the authoritative source with no conflicting DFSR journal wraps.
validation: Confirm the DC's directory content matches the backup's known point-in-time state (spot-check a handful of known test objects) before it is ever reconnected to any wider network.
rollback: If the restore fails validation, discard the VM and re-attempt from the same backup or an earlier verified backup; because the entire drill runs on a disposable isolated VM, rollback is simply reverting to the pre-drill VM snapshot.
cleanup: Revert or delete the lab VM snapshot used for the drill so the next run starts from a known clean state; do not leave an authoritative-restored lab DC connected to any shared lab network afterward without re-isolating it first.

title: Kerberos Ticket Diagnostics Walkthrough
summary: Use klist, nltest, nslookup, and w32tm to diagnose a simulated Kerberos ticket failure end to end, read-only.
objective: Use only read-only diagnostic commands to determine whether a simulated authentication failure is caused by clock skew, DC unavailability, or DNS resolution.
prerequisites_detail: A domain-joined client and target server in a lab domain; ability to intentionally desync the client clock by more than 5 minutes for the drill (a reversible, non-destructive test condition).
environment: Lab domain with one client, one target file/web server, one DC.
topology: Client -> DC (authentication) -> target server (service ticket use).
steps: On the client, run `klist tickets` before attempting access to record the baseline ticket cache.
Deliberately set the client's clock 10 minutes ahead of the DC's clock (lab-only test condition).
Attempt to access the target server and observe the authentication failure.
Run `klist tickets` again and check event logs for KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.
Run `w32tm /resync /computer:<client> /rediscover` to correct the clock, then retry access and confirm success.
Separately, run `nltest /dsgetdc:<domain> /force /kdc` and `nslookup <target-server-name>` to practice the DC-availability and DNS-resolution checks even though this drill's fault was clock skew.
expected_result: Access fails with a clock-skew-related error while desynced, and succeeds immediately after time resync, with klist showing a fresh valid ticket.
validation: Confirm the Security event log on the target server shows a 4624 (success) after resync, versus 4625 or a Kerberos error before it.
rollback: Not applicable - all commands used are read-only diagnostics; the only state change (clock skew) is reversed by the resync step within the lab itself.
cleanup: Confirm the client clock is syncing normally from the domain hierarchy afterward (no manual override left in place).

title: Create and Deploy a gMSA to a Test Service
summary: Create the KDS root key (lab only), create a gMSA, and install it on a test host to run a service.
objective: Provision a gMSA end to end - KDS root key, account creation, host authorization, and use as a scheduled task identity - in a test OU.
prerequisites_detail: Domain functional level Windows Server 2012 or higher; Enterprise Admin rights to create the forest's KDS root key (one-time, lab-safe operation if the forest doesn't already have one); a dedicated test OU.
environment: Lab domain, one member server as the gMSA host.
topology: DC (KDS root key holder) -> test OU containing the gMSA object -> member server authorized to retrieve it.
steps: Check whether a KDS root key already exists: `Get-KdsRootKey`. If none exists in this lab forest, create one for lab use with an immediate-effective time: `Add-KdsRootKey -EffectiveTime ((Get-Date).AddHours(-10))` (production forests should NOT backdate this without following change control - noted here only because it is a disposable lab).
Create a test OU: `New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name 'GMSA-Lab' -Path 'DC=contoso,DC=lab'`.
Create the gMSA, authorizing only the test host to retrieve it: `New-ADServiceAccount -Name svc-lab-gmsa -DNSHostName svc-lab-gmsa.contoso.lab -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword TESTHOST$`.
On the test host, install the account: `Install-ADServiceAccount -Identity svc-lab-gmsa`.
Validate the host can actually use it: `Test-ADServiceAccount -Identity svc-lab-gmsa` (expected: True).
Configure a scheduled task or service on the test host to run as `contoso\svc-lab-gmsa$` with a blank password.
expected_result: Test-ADServiceAccount returns True on the authorized host, and the scheduled task/service starts successfully using the gMSA identity with no password prompt.
validation: Confirm from a second, non-authorized host that Test-ADServiceAccount / Install-ADServiceAccount fails, proving PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword is actually enforced.
rollback: Remove-ADServiceAccount -Identity svc-lab-gmsa to delete the test account; reassign the scheduled task/service back to its prior identity if needed.
cleanup: Remove the test OU and gMSA object; if the KDS root key was created solely for this lab and the lab forest is being decommissioned, no separate cleanup of the root key is required.
